lesson.title: Counting Made Visible: Building a Frequency Table
lesson.summary: A frequency table is the simplest way to display a distribution, listing every value or category alongside a count of how many individuals fall into it.
lesson.body:
A frequency table is the simplest way to display a distribution. It lists every possible value or category of a variable in one column and the frequency, meaning the count of how many individuals had that value, in a second column. Frequency tables turn a distribution, which up to now has only been described in words, into an organized structure that is easy to read, easy to check, and easy to build a graph from.

Constructing a frequency table takes three steps. First, list every distinct value or category that appears in the data, in some sensible order. Second, go through the data and tally how many individuals fall into each category. Third, add the tallies to get a frequency for each row, and check that the frequencies sum to the total number of individuals in the data set. That last check matters: if the frequencies do not add up to the total sample size, a category was miscounted or double counted somewhere.

Suppose 20 students report their eye color: 9 have brown eyes, 6 have blue eyes, 3 have green eyes, and 2 have hazel eyes. The frequency table looks like this. Brown, frequency 9. Blue, frequency 6. Green, frequency 3. Hazel, frequency 2. Adding the frequencies gives 9 plus 6 plus 3 plus 2, which equals 20, matching the total number of students surveyed, so the table is complete and consistent.

Frequency tables work for both categorical variables, like eye color, and quantitative variables, like test scores or number of siblings, as long as the number of distinct values is small enough to list conveniently. When a quantitative variable has many different values spread across a wide range, statisticians often group nearby values into intervals, called classes, before tallying frequencies, which is exactly the idea behind the histogram covered later in this course.

A frequency table is more than a bookkeeping exercise. It is the direct bridge between raw data and the graphs used throughout statistics, because every bar graph, pie chart, and histogram is built by first constructing a frequency table and then drawing a picture whose bars or slices are sized according to those frequencies. Getting comfortable tallying data accurately into a frequency table pays off immediately in every graphing section that follows.

It is also worth noticing what a frequency table does not tell you on its own. Two very different data sets, such as ten students with heights spread fairly evenly from 60 to 70 inches, or ten students where nine are exactly 65 inches tall and one is much taller, could in principle come from populations that behave very differently, even though both would still produce a valid frequency table with frequencies that add up to 10. Reading a frequency table carefully, comparing the actual sizes of the frequencies relative to each other rather than just glancing at the list of categories, is what lets you catch patterns such as one category dominating the data, or a category that appears only rarely, before ever turning the table into a graph.
